Website security basics for business owners

Website security includes the accounts and routines behind the public pages. A small business can reduce avoidable risk by establishing ownership, limiting access, maintaining supported software, and preparing a realistic recovery path.

By Shahir Salehi3 minute readPractical guide

In this guide

  1. Know who controls the domain
  2. Review access deliberately
  3. Maintain what you actually use
  4. Test recovery, not just backup settings
  5. Treat forms as real systems
  6. Use HTTPS and appropriate headers
  7. Prepare for a suspicious event

Know who controls the domain

The domain registrar and DNS provider are critical parts of the website. Record the business owner, renewal responsibility, recovery method, and the people with access. Use strong authentication where supported and avoid sharing a single administrator login. A working website does not prove that the business can regain control if an outside provider becomes unavailable.

Review access deliberately

List hosting, publishing, email, analytics, advertising, form, and store accounts that affect the online presence. Use named accounts and the least access needed for the work. Remove access when responsibilities change. Recovery options should belong to the business and be kept current. Do not store credentials in public source files or send them through ordinary inquiry forms.

Maintain what you actually use

Unsupported software, unused plugins, and forgotten integrations increase uncertainty. Keep an inventory and agree who reviews updates and how they are tested. A static site has fewer runtime components, but still depends on a build toolchain, domain, hosting configuration, and any connected forms or tags. Simpler architecture reduces some maintenance; it does not remove all responsibility.

Test recovery, not just backup settings

A backup is useful only if the right information is included and someone can restore it. Check coverage, retention, access, and separation from the main system. For a static site, preserve source and deployment configuration; for a store, consider orders and product data. Test a representative recovery safely and record the procedure. An enabled backup checkbox is not proof that recovery works.

Treat forms as real systems

A contact form needs server-side validation, spam controls, careful data handling, and clear failure behavior. Public JavaScript cannot keep a secret. Provider credentials belong in the appropriate secure server configuration. Do not send message contents into analytics. If using a challenge service, its result must be verified by the endpoint; a visible checkbox alone does not establish protection.

Use HTTPS and appropriate headers

HTTPS protects data in transit and is essential, but it does not validate every part of the website. Security headers can reduce specific browser risks when they match the implementation. A Content Security Policy should be tested against scripts, fonts, forms, and integrations. Adding restrictive rules without checking behavior can silently break a legitimate journey.

Prepare for a suspicious event

Record who can pause integrations, change access, contact hosting support, and obtain specialist help. Preserve relevant evidence without sharing sensitive logs publicly. If compromise is suspected, avoid ad hoc changes that destroy evidence or spread the problem. A defensive review is not a guarantee against attacks and does not replace dedicated incident response when needed.

Put it into practice

  • Confirm domain and service ownership.
  • Use named accounts and strong authentication.
  • Maintain supported components and remove unused ones.
  • Verify a realistic recovery procedure.
  • Review forms, headers, and incident responsibilities.

Written by Shahir Salehi. This is general educational guidance, not a guarantee of results or individualized legal advice. Platform settings and policies should be checked before implementation.
